content: The chloride ion is created when a chlorine atom gains one electron, resulting in a negatively charged ion, denoted as Cl−. Salts derived from hydrochloric acid (HCl) contain chloride ions and are commonly referred to as chlorides. A well-known example is sodium chloride (NaCl), also known as table salt. When dissolved in water, sodium chloride dissociates into sodium ions (Na+) and chloride ions (Cl−). The term chloride can also describe chemical compounds in which one or more chlorine atoms are covalently bonded within the molecule. These compounds can be either inorganic or organic. For instance, hydrogen chloride (HCl) is the simplest example of an inorganic covalently bonded chloride. An example of an organic covalently bonded chloride, also known as an organochloride, is chloromethane (CH3Cl), commonly referred to as methyl chloride. Other examples of inorganic covalently bonded chlorides that are frequently used as reactants in laboratory settings include: Phosphorus trichloride (PCl3), phosphorus pentachloride (PCl5), and thionyl chloride (SOCl2), all of which are highly reactive chlorinating agents. Disulfur dichloride (S2Cl2), which is utilized in the vulcanization process of rubber. Chloride ions play critical roles in human physiology. In the central nervous system, the inhibitory effects of the neurotransmitter glycine, as well as some of the actions of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), depend on the influx of chloride ions (Cl−) into specific neurons. Additionally, the chloride-bicarbonate exchanger, a biological transport protein, relies on chloride ions to facilitate the transport of carbon dioxide in the blood by converting it into bicarbonate ions. The North American Dietary Reference Intake recommends that 25-year-old males consume between 2300 and 3600 milligrams of chloride per day to meet physiological needs. Beyond its biological significance, chloride serves as a reliable chemical indicator for detecting fecal contamination in rivers and groundwater. This is because chloride is a non-reactive solute that is commonly found in sewage.
